Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I feel on guard even inside my own home
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old woman whose trauma type is stalking, helicopter or aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and maladaptive strategy items all describe hypervigilance, fragmented recall, and interpersonal avoidance consistent with stalking, but no other selected item suggests an aviation-related cue or context. This trigger appears clinically disconnected from the trauma type and from the strong Triggers→Threat / Triggers→Memory pattern in the formulation.

vignette:
Priya was forty-two, a housekeeper who moved between the homes of families in a quiet suburban town. She had been married for eighteen years, and her life had been unremarkable until the stalking began. It started with a man she vaguely recognised-someone who had once been a coworker at a cleaning company. He began appearing outside her workplace, then outside her home. At first she dismissed it, but he grew bolder. One evening he followed her into the laundry room of an apartment building where she was working. He cornered her, his breath sour with alcohol, and made explicit comments about her body, touching himself while staring at her with a look she would never forget. She managed to push past him and flee, but the encounter left her with a bruised shoulder from where he had grabbed her-a pain that throbbed for weeks. The police were called, but the man disappeared before they arrived, and the case eventually stalled for lack of evidence.

In the months that followed, Priya found herself unable to stop scanning the faces of men she passed. Any male gaze-especially those that lingered, or moved down her body-sent a spike of cold fear through her chest, and she would immediately look away, her palms damp, her throat tight. At work, she dreaded entering homes where she knew the male resident would be present. She started avoiding houses where she smelled alcohol on a client's breath or saw empty bottles in recycling bins; the odour alone made her stomach turn and brought back the feel of being trapped. Physical pain also became a trigger. The chronic ache in her shoulder from the assault had faded, but any new pain-a stubbed toe, a pulled muscle-would instantly flood her with the same helpless, trapped sensation. She had come to believe that pain meant vulnerability, that it signalled a moment when she could not protect herself.

Priya began to withdraw from her friends. She feared that if she spent time with them, something terrible would happen-that the man would find her through them, or that they would be hurt because of her. She found herself rehearsing conversations in her head before any interaction, even with her husband, trying to anticipate every possible threat or misunderstanding. At home, she checked the locks on the doors and windows repeatedly, sometimes three or four times before she could settle into sleep. Even inside her own house, she felt on guard, unable to relax. An unusual silence-the furnace not kicking on, the street sounds dying down-would make her freeze, certain that something dangerous was about to happen. She had no coherent story of the assault; when she tried to recall it, the memory fragmented, and she found herself pushing it away before the full image could form. But sometimes, without warning, the taste of something metallic and sour flooded her mouth-the taste of her own fear, she thought, or perhaps the alcohol from his breath-and she would gag, the past rushing back in a sensory wave she could not control.

Her husband noticed the changes. She had stopped inviting friends over, stopped laughing, started sleeping with a knife under the pillow. He asked what was wrong, but she could only say, "I just need you to be safe." She worried obsessively that her husband would be in a car accident, that her elderly mother would have a fall, that any kindness she received would be followed by tragedy. The rehearsed conversations grew longer, more elaborate, as if she could script her life into safety. But the vigilance exhausted her. She was often late to work because she had checked the locks so many times, and one client complained that she seemed "jumpy" and uncomfortable around male family members. Priya said nothing; she simply avoided that client's home.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning when she found herself unable to leave the bedroom. She had heard a car door close outside-a normal sound, the neighbour leaving for work-but the silence that followed felt too heavy, and she sat on the edge of the bed, trembling, the taste already in her mouth. She knew then that she could not go on like this. She wanted to be able to walk past a man without freezing; she wanted to feel safe in her own silence. She wanted, more than anything, to tell the full story of what had happened without the memory dissolving before she could reach the end. But what she feared most was that she would never stop looking over her shoulder, and that one day the taste would stay for good.
